newsitem.title: BERMUDA: Commonwealth meeting opens with call to help poor.
newsitem.headline: Commonwealth meeting opens with call to help poor.

text.p: The world economy may be more integrated, but many of the poorest countries are still under the threat of being left out of the new wealth being created, Commonwealth Secretary General Emeka Anyaoku said on Tuesday.

His comments, at the opening of the group's meeting of finance ministers, echo concerns from member countries that more has to be done to help poor developing nations shake off the almost intolerable burden of debt and give their economies a more hopeful future.

"Many developing countries, including several least developed and small states, have yet to benefit from integration and face the risk of being marginalised in an increasingly competitive world," Anyaoku said.
He pointed to a recent "shocking" report that said the wealth of the world's 358 richest people equalled the combined income of 45 percent of the world's population.
"I believe that this (globalisation) is the key challenge which the international community needs to address in the coming years...global cooperation is imperative," he said.
Debt is the dominant topic at this meeting of some 53 Commonwealth countries.

Many members of the old British Empire are poor and heavily in debt and range from tiny island states such as Nauru, which relies on the export of bird droppings for fertiliser for its livlihood to Asian giant India, as well as wealthy nations such as Canada and Britain.

Anyaoku said there needed to be early resolution of the debt issue, continued adequate amounts of aid, an open international trading environment and measures to deal with the surge in capital flows in and out of developing countries.
A report by the Commonwealth said proposals to bail out countries pushed by debt into deepening poverty are so rigid that very few stand much hope of help before the turn of the century.
Britain has been pressing for greater help, including selling some of the International Monetary Fund's $40 billion in gold reserves, to release funds for the heavily indebted poor countries.
The issue will be one of the main topics at next week's annual IMF/World Bank meeting in Washington when industrial countries will come under further pressure to do more to help the poor.
In his speech, Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer, Kenneth Clarke, urged fellow Commonwealth finance ministers to to press for a resolution of the problem of debt relief at the Washington talks.
"A succesful conclusion is urgently needed," he said.
